scenes.title: What maladaptive daydreaming is
scenes.sub: Definition · lived experience · measurement · who has it
scenes.say: Chapter one. What maladaptive daydreaming actually is, how it is measured, and who has it.

scenes.text: Maladaptive daydreaming is *compulsive, vivid, story-like fantasy* that a person craves, struggles to stop, and lets ~crowd out real life~.
scenes.say: Here is the plain definition. Maladaptive daydreaming, or MD for short, is compulsive, vivid, story-like fantasy. It is often launched on purpose, with music and movement. The person craves it, struggles to stop it, and lets it crowd out real life: work, relationships and sleep.

scenes.head: How the idea developed
items: Somer names it, after treating 6 patients
27 experts: list it as a dissociative disorder
scenes.say: The idea has a short history. In two thousand and two, Eli Somer names it after treating six patients. In twenty eleven, a survey of ninety people calls it compulsive fantasy. In twenty sixteen comes the first scale, tested in forty-five countries. In twenty seventeen, researchers propose formal criteria. And in twenty twenty-five, twenty-seven experts ask for it to be listed as a dissociative disorder.

scenes.text: Extensive fantasy activity that *replaces human interaction* and/or ~interferes with~ academic, interpersonal, or vocational functioning.
scenes.note: A normal childhood talent for imagination, turned into a problem
scenes.say: Somer, a psychologist in Israel, defined it as extensive fantasy activity that replaces human interaction, or interferes with study, relationships or work. He believed it grew from a normal childhood talent for imagination, which hard circumstances turned into a problem.

scenes.head: 2011: ‘compulsive fantasy’
scenes.text: Distress came from *losing control of the urge*, from fantasy ~getting in the way~ of real goals, and from intense shame.
scenes.note: Fantasy filled an estimated 56% of waking hours
scenes.say: In twenty eleven, Bigelsen and Schupak surveyed 90 self-identified fantasizers and proposed the name compulsive fantasy. 79 percent moved their bodies while fantasizing. Their distress came from losing control of the urge, from fantasy getting in the way of real relationships and goals, and from intense shame. They estimated that fantasy filled about 56 percent of their waking hours.

scenes.head: The proposed criteria (2025)
items: Vivid, absorbing fantasy you feel compelled to return to
Plus 2 or more: preferring fantasy · pacing or movement · relief from bad feelings · annoyed when interrupted · failed attempts to stop
At least 30 minutes an episode, 1 hour a day, most days, for 6 months
Not better explained by OCD, ADHD, PTSD or autism
scenes.say: Today's proposed bar, from a twenty twenty-five position paper, has five parts. First, vivid, absorbing fantasy that you feel compelled to return to. Second, at least two extra features: preferring fantasy to reality, pacing or other movement, relief from bad feelings, annoyance when interrupted, or failed attempts to stop. Third, it lasts at least 30 minutes an episode and an hour a day, on most days, for 6 months. Fourth, it causes real distress or impairment. And fifth, nothing else, like OCD, ADHD or PTSD, explains it better.

scenes.head: Features listed in 2017. Sound familiar?
items: Triggered or kept going by music
Triggered or kept going by repetitive movement
Preferring it to chores, study or work
Repeated failed attempts to cut back
scenes.say: The twenty seventeen criteria listed features that may sound familiar. It is triggered or kept going by music, or by repetitive movement. It shows up when you are distressed or bored, and more when you are alone. You get annoyed when interrupted. You prefer it to chores, study or work. And attempts to cut back keep failing. The same paper called it a behavioural addiction to vivid imagery that can last for hours.

scenes.head: From the inside
scenes.text: A rewarding experience based on a created fantasy of a *parallel reality*, with a ~profound sense of presence~.
scenes.say: What does it feel like from the inside? In 21 in-depth interviews, people described a rewarding experience built on a created fantasy of a parallel reality, with a profound sense of presence. Their natural gift for vivid daydreaming had become a time-consuming habit. Being alone was necessary, and music or movement seemed essential.

scenes.head: Typical plots
items: Fantasy worlds that run for years
scenes.say: The plots follow emotional needs, especially competence, recognition and support. Common ones are an idealised version of yourself, fame and success, romance, wish fulfilment, alternate families, and whole fantasy worlds that run for years, with characters ageing over time.

scenes.text: When I am someone *famous* who answers a question in an interview in a very intelligent way.
scenes.note: Success fantasies carry a specific cost (Chapter 4)
scenes.say: Success plots appear explicitly. One person described scenes where, in their words, I am someone famous who answers a question in an interview in a very intelligent way. Keep that one in mind. We will come back to success fantasies, because they carry a specific cost.

scenes.head: Three things recur: reward, ritual, regret
items: Reward: ‘like a drinker who promised himself this is the last bottle’
Ritual: music, solitude and movement set up on purpose, while feeling compelled
Regret: shame and secrecy. Only 23% had ever sought therapy
scenes.say: Across these accounts, three things recur: reward, ritual and regret. The reward is strong enough that a quarter of one sample called it an addiction. One said, I can't turn it off, like a drinker who promised himself this is the last bottle. The ritual is deliberate: people set up music, solitude and movement on purpose, even while feeling compelled. And the regret shows up as shame and secrecy. Only 23 percent had ever sought therapy.
Pause the video if you need to. What three things recur in people's accounts of MD?
scenes.sayA: Reward, ritual and regret. A strong reward, a deliberate ritual, and the regret of shame and secrecy.

scenes.text: For many people, just learning the name ‘*has been utterly life-changing*’.
scenes.note: MD-like patterns appear in classic novels, from Frankenstein to The Great Gatsby
scenes.say: For many people, simply learning that this has a name has been, in one researcher's words, utterly life-changing. And it is not an internet-era invention. An analysis of 20 classic novels, from Frankenstein to The Great Gatsby, found the same patterns long before the internet existed.

scenes.head: How it's measured: the MDS-16 questionnaire
scenes.ev: B · held up in USA, Italy, Turkey, UK
items: Yearning: the pull to go back
scenes.say: The standard screen is a 16-item questionnaire called the MDS-16. It measures four things: yearning, the pull to go back; impairment, what it costs you; kinesthesia, meaning movement; and music. The music items were added because people with MD kept telling researchers how central it was. Across four countries, the most consistent core was interference with daily life and long-term goals.

scenes.text: Original study: a score of 50+ separated cases from controls almost perfectly. ~Real-world screening is messier~: only *60 percent* of positive screens were confirmed by interview.
scenes.note: An Arabic version is validated too (180 people)
scenes.say: In the original study, a score of 50 or more separated confirmed cases from controls almost perfectly. Real-world screening is messier. In population studies, only 60 percent of people who screened positive were confirmed by a clinical interview. And among adults with ADHD, the scale struggles to tell the two conditions apart. An Arabic version has also been validated, with 180 people from several Arab countries.

scenes.text: MD is *not* in the DSM-5-TR or ICD-11. In March 2025, *27 dissociation experts* formally asked for it to be listed as a dissociative disorder.
scenes.note: A high score means ‘possible MD’, not a diagnosis
scenes.say: Officially, MD is not in either psychiatric manual, the DSM or the ICD. In March twenty twenty-five, 27 dissociation researchers and clinicians formally asked for it to be listed as a dissociative disorder. They argue it passes four of the five classic tests of a valid diagnosis. Only lab markers and family studies are missing. There is still no official response. In practice, a high score means possible MD, not a diagnosis, and many clinicians will not know the term.

scenes.text: of adults have MD, confirmed by interview
scenes.sub: 4.4% of students · highest at ages 18 to 30 · no clear female majority
scenes.say: How common is it? The only study that confirmed cases by clinical interview, in Israel, estimates about 2.5 percent of adults. That is 5 in every 200 people. It is about 4.4 percent among students, highest between 18 and 30, with no clear female majority.

scenes.bigl: of people in MD studies are women
scenes.text: That reflects who *joins online communities and volunteers*, not who has MD. A young man with MD is ~not an unusual case~.
scenes.say: Research samples, though, are mostly women, about 76 percent across 40 studies. That reflects who joins online communities and volunteers for surveys, more than who has MD. In the general population there is no clear female majority, so a young man with MD is not an unusual case.

scenes.head: Self-report surveys vs a clinical interview
scenes.say: Surveys of students in Saudi Arabia, the UAE and among Sudanese medical students report much higher figures: 70, 54 and 34 percent. None of them used interviews. Since even stricter screens over-count by about 40 percent, these numbers point to heavy daydreaming under study pressure. The confirmed rate is closer to 2.5 percent.

scenes.head: Common in some clinical groups
scenes.say: It is common in some clinical groups: about 20 percent of adults with ADHD, an estimated 25 to 40 percent of people with dissociative identity disorder, and 49 out of 100 inpatients with dissociative disorders.

scenes.text: It usually *starts in childhood*, and it is ~stable~: over 13 months, 814 people's scores barely moved.
scenes.note: Reddit's MD community alone has 121,000+ members
scenes.say: It usually starts in childhood. And it is stable. When 814 people in Italy were followed for 13 months, their scores barely moved. It is a lasting pattern, not a passing phase. The online community on Reddit alone has more than 121,000 members.

scenes.head: MD is not ordinary mind-wandering
scenes.bigl: of waking hours, everyone's mind wanders
scenes.text: Ordinary mind-wandering is *spontaneous and usually not fanciful*. It helps with planning, creativity and relief from boredom.
scenes.say: Now, everyone's mind wanders. In a study that sampled 2,250 adults about a quarter of a million times, minds wandered 46.9 percent of waking hours, and the wandering seemed to cause later unhappiness more than the reverse. But ordinary mind-wandering is spontaneous and usually not fanciful. It helps with planning, creativity and relief from boredom.

scenes.head: Singer's three daydreaming styles
items: Poor attentional control: can't stay with the thought or the task
scenes.say: The psychologist Jerome Singer described three styles of daydreaming. Positive constructive: playful, wishful, planful and creative. Guilty dysphoric: obsessive, anguished fantasies. And poor attentional control: being unable to stay with either the thought or the task. MD looks like the second and third combined, plus compulsion and impairment. And unlike fantasy proneness, it does not involve confusing fantasy with reality.

scenes.head: How strongly ‘immersive daydreaming’ tracks each
scenes.say: The clearest numbers come from 156 adults diagnosed by interview. An immersive daydreaming factor tracked MD strongly, with a correlation of 0.71, but ordinary mind-wandering only weakly, at 0.31, and ADHD at 0.23. Immersion is the signature of MD.

scenes.head: Three markers of MD
items: Immersion: a deliberate, story-based, emotionally vivid world
Compulsion: yearning, irritation when interrupted, failed attempts to cut back
Cost: lost work, relationships or sleep
scenes.say: So imagination itself is not the problem. Researchers treat a strong talent for immersive daydreaming as a risk factor, not the disorder. Three markers together define the problem. Immersion: a deliberate, story-based, emotionally vivid world. Compulsion: yearning, irritation when interrupted, and failed attempts to cut back. And cost: lost work, relationships or sleep.

scenes.text: The test for any daydream: does it *end in an action*, like a title, a script beat or a plan, or does it ~replace the action~ and keep looping?
scenes.note: Imagination is not the enemy. Unchecked immersion is.
scenes.say: That gives you a simple test for any daydream. Does it end in an action, like a title, a script beat or a plan? Or does it replace the action and keep looping? Imagination is not the enemy. Unchecked immersion is.
Quick check. What are the three markers that separate MD from ordinary mind-wandering?
scenes.sayA: Immersion, compulsion and cost. All three together, not imagination on its own.

scenes.say: And roughly how many adults out of 100 have MD confirmed by a clinical interview?
scenes.sayA: About 2.5 out of 100. Self-report surveys come out far higher, because screens over-count.

scenes.text: Next: *six lenses* on what MD fundamentally is, and what each one means for your focus.
scenes.say: Researchers still argue about what MD fundamentally is. In the next chapter, we will look through six different lenses, and see what each one explains about your own experience.
